items.title: Poverty Line & Expert Committees
items.body:
**In one line:** The poverty line is the level of spending below which a person counts as poor, and a series of expert committees has repeatedly redrawn where that line sits.

**Why it is asked:** The committee sequence and their differing methods (calorie norm versus mixed reference period) are standard factual MCQs.

## Concept

- The **poverty line** is a threshold of per-capita consumption expenditure below which a person is 'poor'. India's traditional line was anchored to a **minimum calorie norm**: **2400 kcal/day (rural)** and **2100 kcal/day (urban)**.
- **Absolute poverty** = inability to meet a fixed subsistence minimum; **relative poverty** = deprivation relative to the rest of society (an inequality concept).
- Measures: **Head Count Ratio (HCR)** = share of population below the line (incidence); **Poverty Gap Index** = average income shortfall of the poor (depth).

## Expert committees

| Committee | Report | Key contribution |
|---|---|---|
| **Alagh** (Task Force) | 1979 | First to define the poverty line using **calorie norms** |
| **Lakdawala** | 1993 | **State-specific** poverty lines; separate rural/urban price indices (CPI-AL, CPI-IW) |
| **Tendulkar** | 2009 | Dropped pure calorie anchor; **Mixed Reference Period (MRP)**; included health & education spend; uniform basket |
| **Rangarajan** | 2014 | Reverted to **separate rural/urban baskets**; **Modified MRP**; govt did not officially adopt |

- **Poverty ratios (2011-12):** Tendulkar ≈ **21.9%** (≈ ₹816/month rural, ₹1000/month urban); Rangarajan ≈ **29.5%** (≈ ₹972/month rural, ₹1407/month urban — about **₹32/day rural and ₹47/day urban** — a costlier basket).

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- Traditional poverty line = calorie norm of 2400 kcal (rural) and 2100 kcal (urban) per person per day.
- Absolute poverty = fixed subsistence minimum; relative poverty = deprivation relative to others.
- Head Count Ratio = incidence (share poor); Poverty Gap = depth (income shortfall).
- Alagh (1979) first defined the calorie-based line; Lakdawala (1993) introduced state-specific lines.
- Tendulkar (2009) used Mixed Reference Period; 21.9% for 2011-12 (~₹816 rural/₹1000 urban per month).
- Rangarajan (2014) used Modified MRP; 29.5% for 2011-12 (~₹972 rural/₹1407 urban per month, ~₹32/₹47 per day); not officially adopted.

items.title: Multidimensional Poverty — Global & National MPI
items.body:
**In one line:** Poverty is more than low income, so the Multidimensional Poverty Index counts the overlapping shortfalls a household faces in health, education and standard of living.

**Why it is asked:** The difference between the global and national MPI, and the sharp fall in India's MPI, are current-affairs favourites.

## Beyond income

Poverty is not only low income; the **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)** captures overlapping **non-monetary deprivations** using the **Alkire-Foster counting method**.

## Global MPI

- Published by **OPHI (University of Oxford)** and **UNDP** (in the Human Development Report since 2010).
- **3 dimensions** — Health, Education, Standard of Living — via **10 indicators**.

## National MPI (NITI Aayog)

- Retains the **3 dimensions** but uses **12 indicators**, adding **Maternal Health** and **Bank Accounts** to reflect India's flagship schemes; based on **NFHS** data.

| Dimension | Indicators |
|---|---|
| Health | Nutrition, Child & adolescent mortality, **Maternal health** |
| Education | Years of schooling, School attendance |
| Standard of living | Cooking fuel, Sanitation, Drinking water, Electricity, Housing, Assets, **Bank account** |

## Key finding

- NITI Aayog's **2023** paper: national MPI headcount fell from **29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23)**, with about **24.82 crore** people escaping multidimensional poverty; largest declines in UP, Bihar and MP.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- MPI uses the Alkire-Foster counting method to measure overlapping deprivations.
- Global MPI = OPHI (Oxford) + UNDP, with 3 dimensions and 10 indicators.
- National MPI (NITI Aayog) keeps 3 dimensions but has 12 indicators — adds maternal health and bank accounts.
- National MPI dimensions: Health, Education, Standard of Living, based on NFHS data.
- NITI 2023: MPI headcount fell 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23); about 24.82 crore escaped poverty.

items.source: OPHI & UNDP Global MPI; NITI Aayog National MPI reports (2021, 2023)

items.title: Types of Unemployment
items.body:
**In one line:** Unemployment comes in distinct forms — from the hidden surplus labour on farms to the skills-mismatch of structural unemployment — and naming each correctly is the exam skill.

**Why it is asked:** Matching each type of unemployment to its example is a recurring question pattern.

## Main types

| Type | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Structural** | Skill-job mismatch from industrial/technological change | Automation displacing assembly-line workers |
| **Frictional** | Short, voluntary gap while switching jobs / first job search | Graduate seeking first job |
| **Cyclical** | Falls in a boom, rises in a recession (demand-linked) | 2008 layoffs in construction/finance |
| **Seasonal** | Tied to particular seasons | Farm labour idle after harvest |
| **Disguised** | More workers engaged than needed; marginal productivity ≈ 0 | Extra family members on a small farm |

## Related forms

- **Open unemployment** — visibly seeking work but jobless.
- **Educated (white-collar) unemployment** — qualified youth unable to find suitable jobs.
- **Technological unemployment** — automation/AI displacing labour.
- **Underemployment** — working below one's capacity, skill or desired hours.

## Lewis model

- W. Arthur Lewis's **dual-sector 'unlimited supply of labour'** model: **surplus (disguised) farm labour** can move to the modern industrial sector at a near-constant wage without cutting farm output — the essence of **structural transformation**. India's **jobless growth** debate questions whether high GDP growth is generating enough jobs.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- Structural unemployment arises from a mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs.
- Frictional unemployment is short-term and voluntary (job transitions); cyclical tracks the business cycle.
- Disguised unemployment: surplus workers whose marginal productivity is near zero, typical of agriculture.
- Educated unemployment affects qualified youth; technological unemployment stems from automation.
- Lewis's dual-sector model transfers surplus farm labour to industry without loss of farm output.
keyPoints: Structural unemployment arises from a mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs.
Frictional unemployment is short-term and voluntary (job transitions); cyclical tracks the business cycle.
Disguised unemployment: surplus workers whose marginal productivity is near zero, typical of agriculture.
Educated unemployment affects qualified youth; technological unemployment stems from automation.
Lewis's dual-sector model transfers surplus farm labour to industry without loss of farm output.
items.mnemonic: 'SF-CSD' warm-up: Structural, Frictional, Cyclical, Seasonal, Disguised.

items.title: Measuring Employment — PLFS
items.body:
**In one line:** The Periodic Labour Force Survey is the government's official source of India's jobs numbers, and it now reports them every month.

**Why it is asked:** PLFS's reference periods and its 2025 monthly revamp are directly examinable.

## What is PLFS

- The **Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS)**, launched by the **NSO (MoSPI) in 2017**, is India's principal source of labour-market data. It **replaced the quinquennial Employment-Unemployment Surveys (EUS)** of the NSSO. First annual report (2019) covered July 2017 – June 2018.

## Measurement approaches

| Approach | Reference period | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Usual Status (UPS/UPSS)** | 365 days | Activity for the major part of the year (+ subsidiary) |
| **Current Weekly Status (CWS)** | 7 days | Employed if works ≥1 hour on any day of the week |
| **Current Daily Status (CDS)** | each day of the week | Most rigorous; captures intensity/underemployment |

- Key ratios: **LFPR** (labour force ÷ population), **WPR** (workers ÷ population), **UR** (unemployed ÷ labour force).

## 2025 revamp (current)

- From **January 2025**, MoSPI revamped the PLFS to release **monthly** labour-force estimates for **both rural and urban** areas (enlarged sample, **calendar-year** reporting), replacing the earlier annual-plus-urban-quarterly design — giving far more timely jobs data.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- PLFS was launched by the NSO (MoSPI) in 2017 and replaced the NSSO's quinquennial EUS.
- Usual Status uses a 365-day reference; CWS uses 7 days; CDS records each day of the week.
- CWS counts a person employed if they work at least one hour on any day of the reference week.
- Key indicators: LFPR (labour force participation), WPR (worker-population ratio), UR (unemployment rate).
- From January 2025, PLFS releases monthly estimates for both rural and urban areas on a calendar-year basis.

items.mnemonic: Reference periods shrink: Usual (year) > Weekly (7 days) > Daily (each day).
items.source: MoSPI — PLFS framework, concepts, and 2024-25 revamp announcement

items.title: Employment & Poverty-Eradication Schemes
items.body:
**In one line:** India tackles poverty and joblessness through wage-work guarantees, skilling and self-employment schemes, with the big recent change being the replacement of MGNREGA in 2025.

**Why it is asked:** Scheme names, their launch years and the MGNREGA-to-VB-G RAM G shift are frequently asked.

## Wage employment — MGNREGA and its successor

- **MGNREGA** (enacted 2005, implemented 2 Feb 2006, Ministry of Rural Development) gave a **legal right to work**: **100 days** of unskilled manual wage employment per rural household per year, with at least one-third of jobs for **women**, an **unemployment allowance** if work is not provided in 15 days, and durable-asset creation.
- Recent tightening: the **Aadhaar-Based Payment System (ABPS)** was made **mandatory from 2024** (job-card ↔ Aadhaar ↔ bank), alongside the **NMMS** app for geo-tagged attendance.
- **Change (2025):** Parliament passed the **Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB–G RAM G)**, which **repealed MGNREGA** and replaced it with an updated rural **employment-and-livelihood guarantee** framework, still under the Ministry of Rural Development.

## Skilling & self-employment

| Scheme | Year | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| **PMEGP** | 2008 | Credit-linked subsidy for micro-enterprises (MSME) |
| **DDU-GKY** | 2014 | Rural youth skilling + placement |
| **Skill India / PMKVY** | 2015 | Vocational training & certification |
| **Stand-Up India** | 2016 | Bank loans to SC/ST & women entrepreneurs |
| **e-Shram** | 2021 | National database of unorganised workers |

## Poverty-eradication lineage

- **Self-employment:** IRDP (1978-80) → **SGSY** (1999) → **NRLM/Aajeevika** (2011) → **DAY-NRLM** (2015).
- **Wage-employment:** NREP/RLEGP → JRY → SGRY → **MGNREGA** → **VB–G RAM G (2025)**.

## Rural credit delivery

- The **Service Area Approach (1989)** was implemented under the **Lead Bank Scheme** (RBI, 1969): each rural/semi-urban bank branch is assigned specific villages for planned credit and development lending — a key channel for anti-poverty credit.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- MGNREGA (2005/2006) gave a legal right to 100 days of wage work; one-third of jobs reserved for women.
- Aadhaar-Based Payment System (ABPS) became mandatory for MGNREGA wages from 2024.
- In 2025 the VB-G RAM G Act repealed MGNREGA and replaced it with an updated rural employment-livelihood framework.
- PMEGP (MSME micro-enterprises), DDU-GKY (rural skilling), Stand-Up India (SC/ST & women loans), e-Shram (unorganised-worker database).
- Self-employment lineage: IRDP (1978-80) to SGSY (1999) to NRLM/DAY-NRLM (2011/2015).
- The Service Area Approach (1989) was implemented under the Lead Bank Scheme (RBI, 1969) for planned rural credit delivery.

items.title: Causes & Current Employment Situation
items.body:
**In one line:** Unemployment in India is driven by a fast-growing labour force meeting too few suitable jobs, and the latest surveys show falling headline rates but a stubborn youth problem.

**Why it is asked:** The causes and the most recent PLFS trend figures feature in both prelims and mains.

## Causes of unemployment in India

- **Population growth** — the labour force grows faster than jobs are created.
- **Education-skill gap** — theoretical curricula, weak vocational training and poor industry-academia linkage leave graduates job-unready (underemployment).
- **Economic factors** — slowdowns, inflation raising production costs, and industrial stagnation depress hiring.
- **Technology** — automation and AI reduce demand for routine manual labour and widen the **digital divide**.

## Current picture (recent PLFS-era trends)

- **Rural-urban shift:** rural unemployment fell markedly from **5.3% (2017-18) to 2.5% (2023-24)**, and urban from **7.7% to 5.1%** over the same period.
- **Youth (15-29)** unemployment remains the key challenge, though it fell from **17.8% (2017-18)** to about **10% (2022-23)**; educated youth are hardest to absorb.
- **Structural features:** dominance of the **informal/unorganised sector**, rising female self-employment, a **low female LFPR** with a wide gender gap, and sharp **regional disparities** across states.
- The **jobless growth** debate asks whether high GDP growth is generating proportionate employment.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- Main causes: population growth, education-skill mismatch, economic slowdowns/inflation, and automation.
- Rural unemployment fell from 5.3% (2017-18) to 2.5% (2023-24); urban from 7.7% to 5.1%.
- Youth (15-29) unemployment fell from 17.8% (2017-18) to about 10% (2022-23) but remains the core challenge.
- India's labour market is dominated by the informal/unorganised sector with a low female LFPR.
- Jobless growth = GDP growth not matched by proportionate job creation; regional disparities are wide.

items.title: For Mains — Poverty & Unemployment
items.body:
Poverty and unemployment feed **Paper-IV (Economy & Development)**, especially the **'inclusive growth'** clause (poverty alleviation, financial inclusion). Examiners want measurement debates + policy evaluation, not scheme lists.

| Dimension | Content to deploy |
|---|---|
| **Measurement** | Calorie line → Tendulkar/Rangarajan income lines → multidimensional (MPI) |
| **Nature of unemployment** | Disguised (agri), structural, educated, technological; jobless growth |
| **Causes** | Labour-force growth, skill gap, informality, low female LFPR |
| **Interventions** | Wage guarantee (MGNREGA→VB-G RAM G), skilling (PMKVY/DDU-GKY), self-employment (PMEGP, NRLM), e-Shram |
| **Criticism / way forward** | Leakages, placement quality; labour-intensive manufacturing + formalisation + female participation |

**Data points & authorities to quote:** National MPI headcount **29.17% (2013-14) → 11.28% (2022-23)**, ~**24.82 crore** escaped (NITI 2024); Tendulkar **21.9%** vs Rangarajan **29.5%** (2011-12); **PLFS monthly from Jan 2025**; World Bank: ~**171 million** lifted from extreme poverty (2011-12 to 2022-23), extreme poverty ~**5.3%**; MGNREGA **repealed by the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025**; Alkire-Foster method; **Amartya Sen** (capability deprivation), **Arthur Lewis** (surplus labour), **Mahbub-ul-Haq**.

**AP angle:** Andhra Pradesh combines a large informal/agrarian workforce with highly digitised welfare delivery (DBT, Navaratnalu-type schemes); its aquaculture, horticulture and services sectors are the natural absorbers of disguised rural underemployment, and MPI-indicator tracking aligns with its service-delivery platforms.

**Use in answers:** (1) open by separating *income poverty* from *multidimensional deprivation*; (2) use the **committee-timeline table (Alagh→Rangarajan)** and the **MPI decline figures** as evidence; (3) evaluate the MGNREGA→VB-G RAM G shift on whether it keeps the justiciable guarantee; (4) close with Sen's 'development as freedom' and the need for employment-rich, inclusive growth.
keyPoints: Frame: measurement debate (income vs MPI) + nature/causes of unemployment + policy evaluation.
Quote MPI 29.17%→11.28% (2022-23), ~24.82 cr escaped; Tendulkar 21.9% vs Rangarajan 29.5%.
Current reforms: PLFS monthly from Jan 2025; MGNREGA repealed by VB-G RAM G Act 2025.
Thinkers: Sen (capability deprivation), Lewis (surplus labour), Alkire-Foster (MPI method).
AP angle: digitised welfare delivery + aquaculture/horticulture/services absorbing rural underemployment.
items.source: NITI Aayog National MPI (2024); World Bank poverty data; MoSPI PLFS; Ministry of Rural Development (VB-G RAM G Act 2025)
